Billericay.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Essex
s1loc: Billericay trades on a long market-town history that reaches back to Roman times and the Mayflower Pilgrims, who left from the town for the New World in 1620. The High Street still runs as the heart of the town, lined with independent shops, cafes and the Chantry House, while Norsey Wood, an ancient 165-acre woodland tied to the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, pulls walkers in for its famous spring bluebells.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Lake Meadows, a 40-acre park built around a lake dug out in the 1930s on the old Spitty estate, with a play area, tennis courts, skate park, bowling club and lakeside cafe. Just outside town, Barleylands Farm Park at Billericay draws families to its animal barns, craft village and miniature railway, a fixture of the seasonal day-trip trade.

Heritage and culture run through the Cater Museum on the High Street, which tells the town's story from the Mayflower link onwards, alongside the Emmaus Christian Centre and the Burstead and Billericay parish churches. The town's summer fairs and the long-running events on Lake Meadows keep an outdoor calendar busy through the warmer months, drawing visitors from across the Basildon district.

Underpinning the trade is Billericay's commuter rail line into London Liverpool Street and easy reach of the A12 and A127, putting the wider south Essex draw within a short drive. The hotel and guest-house base, the country pubs around Stock and Galleywood and the proximity of Hadleigh Castle and the Essex coast keep tour operators and small activity centres working across the year.

Coalville.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north-west Leicestershire
s1loc: Coalville sits at the heart of the National Forest, the ambitious replanting of 200 square miles of former coalfield across Leicestershire, Derbyshire and Staffordshire. The town grew on mining, and the old Snibston Colliery site has been reclaimed as Snibston Colliery Park, with scheduled ancient colliery buildings, a 100-acre country park and the Grange Nature Reserve, once the colliery manager's garden, with its Victorian arboretum and wildflower meadows.

The leisure and activity layer is anchored by Conkers near Moira, a flagship National Forest attraction with indoor and outdoor exhibits, a treetop walkway, adventure play and a miniature railway. Bardon Hill, the highest point in Leicestershire at 278 metres, rewards walkers with views over Charnwood Forest, while the Hermitage and Whitwick leisure facilities and nearby Donington Park circuit add to the activity draw.

Heritage and culture centre on the Century Theatre at Snibston, Britain's oldest surviving travelling theatre, built from ex-RAF trailers in 1952 and now a permanent venue for drama, comedy, music and film. Nearby Mount St Bernard Abbey, the first permanent monastery founded in England since the Reformation in 1835, draws visitors to its Trappist monks, who brew the only Trappist beer in Britain.

Underpinning the trade are the town's road links along the A511 and easy reach of the M1 and M42, putting Leicester, Loughborough and the wider East Midlands within a short drive. The growing cluster of forest lodges, holiday cabins and country pubs across the National Forest, plus walking and cycling operators on the reclaimed pit landscapes, keeps the seasonal day-trip trade busy through the year.

Hitchin.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north Hertfordshire
s1loc: Hitchin draws its marquee appeal from Hitchin Lavender at Ickleford, where rows of purple blooms and a sunflower field cover sweeping farmland on the edge of the Chilterns, pulling in pick-your-own visitors through high summer. The medieval Market Place and St Mary's Church, one of the largest parish churches in Hertfordshire and dating from the 12th century, anchor a town centre rich with independent shops and old coaching inns.

The leisure and activity layer runs from Hitchin Market, one of the largest outdoor markets in the region with antique, craft and farmers' days, to the green expanse of Bancroft Gardens and the Priory and Windmill Hill open spaces. Walking and cycling routes out into the Chilterns National Landscape and the lavender and wildflower fields keep activity operators busy across the warmer months.

Heritage and culture centre on the British Schools Museum, set in an original 19th-century school building with a Victorian classroom visitors can sit in, alongside the Hitchin Museum collections and the long-running Market Theatre. The three-week Hitchin Festival each July fills the town with concerts, theatre, ghost walks and fireworks, building on the legacy of the Rhythms of the World world-music festival.

Underpinning the trade is Hitchin's fast rail line into London King's Cross and easy reach of the A1(M), with London Luton Airport close by for inbound visitors. The hotel and guest-house base, the country pubs of the surrounding villages and the day-trip pull of Letchworth Garden City and the wider Chilterns keep tour operators and small activity centres working through the seasons.

Dunstable.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Bedfordshire
s1loc: Dunstable is best known for ZSL Whipsnade Zoo, set in 600 acres of Chiltern countryside overlooking the Downs, home to thousands of animals and the giant chalk-cut Whipsnade White Lion on the hillside. The town itself grew as a medieval staging post on Watling Street, and the Priory Church of St Peter, the surviving part of Dunstable Priory founded in 1132, remains the great landmark of the old town centre.

The leisure and activity layer is centred on Dunstable Downs, a chalk-grassland Site of Special Scientific Interest in the Chiltern Hills famous for kite flying, paragliding and hang gliding, with the London Gliding Club based at the foot of the slopes. The National Trust visitor centre, the Five Knolls ancient barrows and the nearby Tree Cathedral at Whipsnade add quiet walking and family draws across the year.

Heritage and culture run through the 780-seat Grove Theatre in the town centre, one of the area's premier entertainment venues, alongside the Priory House heritage centre and the medieval Eleanor Cross history tied to the town. The surrounding villages, the Ashridge Estate and College Lake nature reserve broaden the events and day-trip calendar for visitors basing themselves in the town.

Underpinning the trade are Dunstable's links along the A5 and M1 and the guided busway connecting Houghton Regis, Dunstable and Luton through to London Luton Airport, putting inbound visitors within easy reach. The hotel base across the town and Luton corridor, the country pubs of the Chilterns and the pull of Whipsnade and the Downs keep tour operators and small activity centres working through the seasons.

Wickford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Essex
s1loc: Wickford grew from a Saxon farming village with a livestock market into a busy commuter town after the railway arrived in the 1880s, its name tied to a winding river and a shallow ford. The town centre still holds a regular street market, and the surrounding countryside carries deep history, from Roman and Saxon settlement to a part in the Peasants' Revolt, giving the town a quiet heritage backdrop to its day-to-day trade.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Wick Country Park, a 50-acre reserve opened in 2005 on former farmland with over two kilometres of accessible trails, old hedgerows, a five-acre lake, ponds and surviving WWII pillboxes. Wickford Memorial Park, established in 1946 across 110 acres with its Avenue of Remembrance, woodland, wildflower meadow, community orchard and sports pitches, adds further open-air draw.

Heritage and culture run through the Avenue of Remembrance and the memorial wall at Wickford Memorial Park, St Catherine's parish church and the town's long market tradition since the Saxon livestock days. Nearby Barleylands Farm Park near Billericay, with its animal barns, craft village and family activities, and the events held across Wick Country Park broaden the seasonal calendar for visitors exploring the Basildon and Rayleigh district.

Underpinning the trade is Wickford's rail line into London Liverpool Street and easy reach of the A127 and A130, putting Basildon, Rayleigh and the Essex coast within a short drive. The guest-house and country-pub base, the proximity of Hadleigh Castle and the Thames Estuary views, and the wildlife draw of the country parks keep tour operators and small activity centres working across the year.

Bridlington.region: Bridlington and the East Yorkshire coast
Bridlington.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the East Yorkshire coast
s1loc: Bridlington is one of the East Yorkshire coast's great seaside resorts, set around Bridlington Harbour alive with fishing boats and pleasure cruises and known as the largest lobster port in Europe. Its two sweeping beaches, the rugged North Beach below the cliffs and the soft golden sands of South Beach, frame a town on the Holderness coast that has drawn Yorkshire holidaymakers for generations along the Royal Princess and Yorkshire Belle pleasure routes.

The leisure and activity layer runs from Sewerby Hall and Gardens, a Grade I listed country house of 1714 set in 50 cliff-top acres with a zoo, gardens and woodland walks, to Bondville Model Village with its 200 miniature buildings and working trains. The land train from the Leisure World seafront up to Sewerby, watersports off South Beach and the dramatic cliffs of Flamborough Head keep activity operators busy through the season.

Heritage and culture centre on Bridlington Priory, a Grade I listed church on the site of an Augustinian house dating from 1113, and the Bridlington Spa, a historic seafront venue hosting concerts, theatre and events year round. The popular 1940s Festival each June and the town's kite festival and seafront events fill an outdoor calendar that draws visitors well beyond the school holidays.

Underpinning the trade is a deep base of seafront hotels, guest houses and the Old Town's accommodation, served by rail links via Hull and Scarborough and the A165 coast road. The lobster and crab fleet, the RNLI lifeboat station, the cliff scenery of Flamborough and Bempton and the wider Yorkshire Wolds day-trip country keep tour operators and small activity centres trading hard through the season.

Beverley.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of East Yorkshire
s1loc: Beverley is one of England's finest historic market towns, crowned by Beverley Minster, a vast Gothic church built around the tomb of Saint John of Beverley and completed in 1425 after more than 200 years of building. The medieval North Bar, the last surviving town gate, and the twin Saturday and Wednesday Markets give the centre a rich, proper streetscape of Georgian frontages and ancient lanes.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the Westwood, a vast common pasture grazed by cattle where Beverley Racecourse has run flat racing for over 300 years between April and September. The golf course on the Westwood, the open walking country on the edge of the Yorkshire Wolds and the racecourse fixtures give activity operators and day-trippers a steady draw across the warmer months.

Heritage and culture run through the Treasure House, opened in 2007 to hold the museum, library and archives, and the Beverley Art Gallery with its works by Fred and Mary Elwell, Russell Flint and Laura Knight. The Beverley Folk Festival each June, running since 1983, fills venues across the town with traditional and contemporary folk music, anchoring a year-round events and festival calendar.

Underpinning the trade is Beverley's rail line via Hull, bringing visitors from London and Manchester in around three hours, and easy reach of the A1079 and the wider East Riding. The hotel and guest-house base around the Minster and Market areas, the country pubs of the Wolds villages and the day-trip pull of Hull and the Bridlington coast keep tour operators and small activity centres working through the seasons.
